etymology: From the Old French arreer, to put in order, and that from a Late Latin compound of ad and a Germanic root meaning to make ready — whence also array, the ordered ranks of an army. To array is to clothe in order and dignity, not merely to cover.
biblical_def: To be arrayed is to be clothed by another’s hand, and Scripture makes the arraying a matter of who does the clothing. Pharaoh “arrayed him in vestures of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck” (Gen 41:42), and Joseph goes from the dungeon to the second chariot in a single verse; the robe is the visible token of an office he did not seize. Haman is compelled to array Mordecai and lead his horse through the street (Est 6:11), which is one of the sharpest reversals in Scripture — the man who built the gallows dresses the man he meant to hang. Our Lord uses the word to end all anxiety about clothing: “even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29). The lily is better dressed than the richest king in Israel’s history, and it neither toils nor spins; therefore the God who arrays a flower for a day will not neglect His children. And the word reaches its end in the marriage of the Lamb, where the bride is “arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints” (Rev 19:8) — and the text carefully says it was granted to her. Even the white she wears at the wedding is a gift. From Joseph to the bride, no one in Scripture arrays himself.
webster_summary: Clothed, dressed, or adorned, especially with dignity or in order; also, drawn up in ranks. In Scripture, always the clothing put on by another’s hand.
webster_full: ARRAY, v.t. To place or dispose in order, as troops for battle.
To deck or dress; to adorn with dress; applied especially to rich or splendid garments.
From the Old French arreer, to put in order, to make ready.
ARRAYED, pp. Clothed; adorned; drawn up in order.
In law, to set a jury in order for the trial of a cause.
scriptures: And Pharaoh took off his ring from his hand, and put it upon Joseph's hand, and arrayed him in vestures of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck;
Est 6:11

Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.
Mat 6:29
And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
Rev 19:8
And to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints.
corruption_summary: The self-made man is the age’s ideal, and he is precisely the man Scripture never shows — every arraying in the Bible is done by a hand other than the wearer’s.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is self-investiture. The reigning story of our time is the one in which a man rises by his own effort, robes himself in an honour he has earned, and owes the credit to nobody. Scripture tells no such story. Joseph is arrayed by Pharaoh, Mordecai by Haman’s unwilling hands, the lilies by God, the bride by grant. Even the high priest was washed and clothed by Moses at his consecration; he did not vest himself. The pattern is so consistent that it amounts to a doctrine: honour is conferred, never assumed, and the man who dresses himself in a dignity no one gave him is an impostor however fine the cloth.

Recover the plain sense: the doctrine of imputed righteousness stands or falls here. Rev 19:8 says the bride’s fine linen is the righteousness of saints, and in the same breath that it was granted to her — the works are truly hers and the ability to do them was given. Set that against the filthy rags of Isa 64:6 and the wedding garment of Mat 22:11, where a man is cast out for attending in his own clothes. The gospel does not ask a sinner to improve his wardrobe. It strips him and arrays him, and the shame of the stripping is the price of the robe. Mat 6:29 then applies the comfort at the humblest level: a Father who dresses grass will dress you.
roots_summary: Old French arreer, to set in order — clothing conferred by another’s hand, never assumed by the wearer.
roots_lines: Arrayed — Old French arreer, to put in order, make ready.
The same word gives the military array, ranks set in order.
Gen 41:42: the robe is the token of a conferred office.
Mat 6:29: the lily outdresses Solomon without toiling or spinning.
Rev 19:8: the bride’s linen is hers, and was granted to her.
usage: No one in Scripture arrays himself — the hand is always another’s.
Est 6:11: Haman must array the man he built a gallows for.
Rev 19:8 holds imputed righteousness and real works together in one verse.

etymology: From the Latin cancer, a crab, and thence a spreading ulcer or corroding sore — through the Old French chancre. To be cankered is to be eaten through by a corrosion working from within, whether rust in metal or gangrene in flesh.
biblical_def: Cankered appears once in Scripture, and it is a thunderclap: “Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire” (Jas 5:3). Take the image exactly as James gives it. Gold and silver do not properly rust; the metal is chosen for money precisely because it does not corrode. So the picture is deliberately impossible — treasure that has been hoarded so long that even incorruptible metal has been eaten through, wealth kept past all use until it rots in the keeping. And the rust is not merely loss; it is a witness, a legal term. The corrosion will stand up in court and testify against the man who owned it. What convicts him is not that he had money but that he hoarded it in the last days while the hire of his labourers was kept back by fraud and cried in the ears of the Lord of sabaoth. James is not preaching against wealth as such; Abraham was rich and Job was richer. He is preaching against the accumulation that serves nothing and no one, and he says its own decay will accuse it. Set beside our Lord’s words in Mat 6:19 — treasure on earth where moth and rust doth corrupt — and the lesson is that earthly treasure is not merely insecure. It is actively decomposing while its owner counts it.
webster_summary: Corroded, rusted, or eaten through by a spreading decay; figuratively, corrupted or made malignant from within.
webster_full: CANKER, n. A corroding or gangrenous sore; a spreading ulcer.
Rust upon metal; anything that corrodes, corrupts, or consumes by degrees.
From the Latin cancer, a crab, and hence a spreading ulcer; Old French chancre.
CANKERED, pp. Corroded; corrupted; grown rusty or malignant.
Figuratively, of the temper: crabbed, soured, malignant.
scriptures: Jas 5:1
Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you.
Jas 5:3
Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days.
Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
corruption_summary: Hoarding has been rebranded as prudence and stewardship, so the exact practice James says will testify in court is now recommended from pulpits as wisdom.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the baptism of accumulation. Because Scripture genuinely commends foresight — the ant provideth her meat in the summer, a good man leaveth an inheritance to his children’s children, and he that provideth not for his own is worse than an infidel — it is easy to file every degree of hoarding under prudence and never ask where provision ends and heaping begins. James supplies the test, and it is not a percentage. It is twofold: what is the treasure doing, and what is being withheld to build it? His rich men are condemned in the same paragraph for keeping back the hire of the labourers. The gold rotted in the vault while wages went unpaid, and the two facts belong to one indictment.

Recover the plain sense: money is a tool and a trust, and a tool that is never used is not being preserved but wasted. Our Lord does not forbid treasure; He relocates it — lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven — and the whole argument turns on where a thing is safe. Earthly treasure is not merely at risk from moth, rust, and thieves; James says it is decaying in the hand that holds it, and the decay is admissible evidence. The searching question is not how much do I have but what is it for, and who is going short while I keep it?
roots_summary: Latin cancer, a spreading sore — corrosion working from within; in James, hoarded wealth whose own rust testifies in court.
roots_lines: Cankered — Latin cancer, a crab, hence a spreading ulcer; Old French chancre.
Used of rust in metal and of gangrene in flesh alike.
Jas 5:3: gold and silver do not naturally rust — the image is deliberately impossible.
The rust is a witness, a legal term: the corrosion testifies against its owner.
Paired with Mat 6:19, where moth and rust corrupt earthly treasure.
usage: James condemns hoarding, not wealth; Abraham and Job were rich men.
The indictment joins rotting treasure to withheld wages (Jas 5:4).
Mat 6:20: treasure is not forbidden but relocated.

etymology: From the Old French chaufer, to warm, and that from the Latin calefacere, to make hot — calidus, warm, and facere, to make. To chafe is first to heat by rubbing, then to fret, and at last to be inflamed in temper.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, in a passage of shrewd military counsel: Hushai warns Absalom that David and his men “be mighty men, and they be chafed in their minds, as a bear robbed of her whelps in the field” (2Sa 17:8). The etymology does the preaching. To be chafed is to be heated by rubbing, and the figure is exact — these were not men in a sudden rage but men worn raw by continual friction, driven from the city, hunted, cursed by Shimei, and now fighting for their lives. Hushai’s point is that such men are the most dangerous of all opponents, because grief has been rubbed into fury and they have nothing left to lose. He borrows Solomon’s proverb for the image: “Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man, rather than a fool in his folly” (Pro 17:12). The counsel is offered as flattery and is in truth a trap, for Hushai speaks to delay Absalom until David can cross Jordan, and the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel. Yet the observation itself is sound and worth a Christian’s notice. Anger that is rubbed rather than kindled is the most durable kind, and Scripture accordingly sets a curfew on it: “let not the sun go down upon your wrath” (Eph 4:26).
webster_summary: Heated or made sore by rubbing; hence fretted, irritated, or inflamed in temper. Used of men worn raw by continual provocation.
webster_full: CHAFE, v.t. To excite heat by friction; to rub in order to warm.
To fret and wear by rubbing; as, to chafe the skin.
To irritate; to excite heat in the temper; to enrage.
From the Old French chaufer; Latin calefacere, to make warm.
CHAFED, pp. Made sore by rubbing; fretted; irritated; angered.
scriptures: For, said Hushai, thou knowest thy father and his men, that they be mighty men, and they be chafed in their minds, as a bear robbed of her whelps in the field: and thy father is a man of war, and will not lodge with the people.
Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man, rather than a fool in his folly.
Eph 4:26
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
corruption_summary: Chronic irritation is now treated as a personality trait or a symptom to be managed, rather than as wrath in a slow form — which is how Scripture treats it, curfew and all.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the excusing of the slow burn. Sudden rage is still generally condemned; the settled, simmering irritability of a man perpetually chafed is not, and is often accepted as temperament, stress, or the natural residue of a hard life. Scripture makes no such allowance. Eph 4:26 places a deadline on anger precisely because anger left overnight ceases to be an event and becomes a condition, and the next verse names the danger without softening it: neither give place to the devil. What begins as a justified grievance, rubbed daily, becomes the raw place through which the adversary gets a foothold.

Recover the plain sense: the friction is often real and the provocation genuine — David’s men had been genuinely wronged. The command is not to deny the rubbing but to refuse to let it become a permanent inflammation. He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city (Pro 16:32). Note that Solomon rates self-rule above conquest, which is the exact reverse of the world’s scale. And note who is finally described as chafed in 2 Samuel: men who had followed David faithfully and were nonetheless being consumed by their own bitterness. Faithfulness under injury does not by itself protect the heart; it must be guarded daily, before sundown.
roots_summary: Latin calefacere, to make hot — heat by friction; anger produced by rubbing rather than by sudden kindling.
roots_lines: Chafed — Old French chaufer, Latin calefacere, to make warm.
First of the skin, worn raw by rubbing; then of the temper.
2Sa 17:8: chafed in their minds, as a bear robbed of her whelps.
Hushai’s counsel is a delaying trap, though the observation is sound.
Eph 4:26 sets a sundown curfew on wrath, lest friction become a foothold.
usage: The image is friction, not flame — anger rubbed in, not suddenly kindled.
Pro 17:12 supplies the bear; Hushai borrows it to frighten Absalom.
Eph 4:26–27: anger kept overnight gives place to the devil.

etymology: From the Old French dauber, to plaster or whitewash, and that from the Latin dealbare, to whiten — de, intensive, and albus, white. To daub is to smear a coating over a surface, covering what is beneath rather than mending it.
biblical_def: Daub is the prophet’s word for a cosmetic ministry. Ezekiel is sent against men who built a flimsy wall and then covered it: “one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter” (Eze 13:10). Untempered mortar is plaster without the binding that makes mortar hold — it looks like masonry and has no strength whatever. The wall is Israel’s false peace, and the daubers are the prophets who said Peace; and there was no peace. Their whole trade was to make an unsound structure look sound. God’s answer is not to argue with the plaster but to send weather: “there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall” (Eze 13:11), and “I will break down the wall that ye have daubed with untempered morter” (Eze 13:14). The storm is sent expressly to test the wall, and when it falls the daubers fall with it — for they are standing inside their own work. Our Lord uses the same picture against the scribes and Pharisees: “ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones” (Mat 23:27). Whitewash over a tomb, plaster over a crack, peace where there is no peace — one sin with three faces, and God sends rain against all of them.
webster_summary: To smear or plaster over, especially so as to conceal a defect; hence, to cover an unsound thing with a fair appearance.
webster_full: DAUB, v.t. To smear with soft adhesive matter; to plaster; to cover with mud or clay.
To paint coarsely or without skill; hence, a daub, a poor painting.
To disguise with a specious covering; to flatter grossly.
From the Old French dauber, to plaster; Latin dealbare, to whiten, from albus, white.
Untempered morter (Eze 13:10) is plaster lacking the binding that gives mortar strength.
scriptures: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter:
Say unto them which daub it with untempered morter, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones , shall fall; and a stormy wind shall rend it.

So will I break down the wall that ye have daubed with untempered morter, and bring it down to the ground, so that the foundation thereof shall be discovered, and it shall fall, and ye shall be consumed in the midst thereof: and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness.
corruption_summary: The daubing trade is thriving: a ministry that manages perception, reassures the unconverted, and treats a congregation’s comfort as the measure of its health is doing exactly what Ezekiel’s false prophets did.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the ministry of reassurance. It is a settled instinct in fallen men to prefer the plasterer to the builder, and Ezekiel’s daubers were popular precisely because they said what the people wished to hear. The modern forms are easy to name: preaching that never troubles a conscience, counselling that soothes without ever calling sin by its name, church discipline abandoned lest anyone be distressed, and the steady substitution of the word encouragement for the word truth. The seduction is the more dangerous because the plaster is genuinely attractive. A daubed wall looks better than an honest one; that is the entire point.

Recover the plain sense: God’s remedy is weather. He does not debate the plaster; He sends an overflowing shower and great hailstones, and the wall goes down — and Ezekiel is careful to say the daubers perish in it, because a man who spends his life making unsound things look sound is finally sheltering under his own work. The mercy in the storm is that it comes now rather than later. Better a wall thrown down in time than a false peace held until the day of judgment. The builder’s work is slower and plainer, and it is the only kind that stands: preach the whole counsel of God, name sin, and let the comfort be the comfort of the gospel and not of whitewash.
roots_summary: Latin dealbare, to whiten — to plaster over an unsound thing; the prophets’ word for a ministry of false peace.
roots_lines: Daub — Old French dauber, from Latin dealbare, to whiten.
The same root gives albino and album, from albus, white.
Untempered morter: plaster without binding — the look of masonry, none of the strength.
Eze 13:10–15: God sends weather to test the wall, and the daubers fall with it.
Mat 23:27: the whited sepulchre is the same sin applied to a man.
usage: The wall in Eze 13 is a false peace; the daubers are the prophets who made it look safe.
Untempered mortar has the appearance of strength and none of the substance.
God’s answer to daubing is a storm sent expressly to test the wall.

etymology: From the Old French forbir, to polish or burnish, of Germanic origin. To furbish is to scour a weapon bright — not to sharpen its edge but to polish its surface, so that it flashes and slides clean.
biblical_def: To furbish is to burnish a blade for battle, and Scripture uses it in two directions. Jeremiah cries it as a taunt to Egypt mustering at Carchemish: “Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines” (Jer 46:4). The commands are given in earnest and the next verse answers them — Wherefore have I seen them dismayed and turned away back? Let Egypt polish every spear she owns; the LORD has appointed the day, and burnished steel will not alter it. The other direction is more solemn, for the sword being furbished is God’s own: “A sword, a sword is sharpened, and also furbished” (Eze 21:9), and again, “he hath given it to be furbished, that it may be handled” (Eze 21:11). Mark the passive — the sword is given to be polished, prepared by God’s appointment and put into a hand He chooses. Babylon is the hand; the LORD is the armourer. This is the doctrine of providence at its hardest edge: the instruments of judgment are not merely permitted, they are prepared, polished, and delivered. A furbished sword also shines, and the shining is part of its terror. Judgment in Scripture is rarely secret; it is made to glitter before it falls.
webster_summary: To polish, burnish, or scour bright, as armour or a weapon; to rub up so as to restore lustre.
webster_full: FURBISH, v.t. To rub or scour to brightness; to polish; to burnish.
To make bright by rubbing, as arms or armour before a battle.
From the Old French forbir, to polish; of Germanic origin.
Distinguished from sharpening: furbishing brightens the surface, whetting gives the edge.
Eze 21:9 joins both: the sword is sharpened, and also furbished.
scriptures: Jer 46:4
Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines.
Jer 46:5
Wherefore have I seen them dismayed and turned away back? and their mighty ones are beaten down, and are fled apace, and look not back: for fear was round about, saith the LORD.
Eze 21:9
Son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus saith the LORD; Say, A sword, a sword is sharpened, and also furbished:
And he hath given it to be furbished, that it may be handled : this sword is sharpened, and it is furbished, to give it into the hand of the slayer.
corruption_summary: Preparation is mistaken for security — Egypt was told to furbish her spears and was routed anyway, because no amount of readiness overrules a day the LORD has appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The abiding temptation the word exposes is trust in preparation. Jer 46:4 reads like a rousing muster: harness, mount, stand forth, polish the spears, put on the armour. Everything a competent army should do, Egypt did. And the very next verse asks why they are seen dismayed and turned back, fleeing apace and not looking behind. Scripture does not despise preparation — the horse is prepared against the day of battle — but it refuses to let preparation become the ground of confidence, because safety is of the LORD. The modern equivalents are obvious enough: the plan, the reserve, the policy, the credential, each good in its place and each ruinous the moment it becomes the thing trusted.

Recover the plain sense: furbish your spears, and know who appoints the day. The believer is commanded to take the whole armour of God, to watch, to be sober, to give diligence — there is no piety in negligence. But Eze 21 shows the other half, and it is the half that steadies a Christian in a dark providence. The sword that falls is a sword God had furbished; the instrument of judgment did not slip out of His hand into someone else’s. Whatever blade is glittering over a nation or a household, it was polished by appointment, and the God who prepared it is the God who says how far it goes.
roots_summary: Old French forbir, to polish — a weapon scoured bright for battle; in Ezekiel, the sword God Himself prepares and delivers.
roots_lines: Furbish — Old French forbir, to burnish or polish.
To brighten the surface, distinct from whetting, which gives the edge.
Jer 46:4: Egypt is told to furbish her spears — and is routed regardless.
Eze 21:9–11: the sword is sharpened, furbished, and given to be handled.
A furbished blade shines; judgment in Scripture is made to glitter before it falls.
usage: Jer 46:4–5: full preparation followed immediately by rout — the day is the LORD’s.
Eze 21:11 uses the divine passive: the sword is given to be furbished.
Furbishing polishes; whetting sharpens. Eze 21:9 names both.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s contracted spelling of stripped, from the Saxon strypan, to plunder or despoil. The root sense is not undressing but robbing — to strip a man is to take from him what was his covering.
biblical_def: The verse is one of the coldest in Genesis: “when Joseph was come unto his brethren, that they stript Joseph out of his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him” (Gen 37:23). The narrator lingers deliberately — his coat, his coat of many colours, that was on him — because the garment is the whole quarrel. Israel had made it for him as the token of a favour the brothers could not bear (Gen 37:3), and stripping it off is the first act of the crime; the pit and the sale follow. They did not merely rob him of cloth. They tore off the sign of his father’s love, and then dipped it in goat’s blood and sent it back, so that the father might read his son’s death in the token of his own affection. Yet the arc of Joseph’s life is the reversal of that stripping: the man torn out of his coat is arrayed by Pharaoh in vestures of fine linen (Gen 41:42), and the brothers who stripped him bow before the robe they never gave. The same word governs the parable of the man who went down to Jericho and fell among thieves, “which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead” (Luk 10:30) — and it is a Samaritan, not a priest, who covers him. Scripture strips men only to clothe them better.
webster_summary: Deprived of covering; despoiled or plundered. The Authorized Version’s contracted form of stripped, carrying the root sense of robbery rather than mere undressing.
webster_full: STRIP, v.t. To pull or tear off, as a covering; to deprive of a covering.
To deprive; to divest; to make destitute; to plunder or pillage.
From the Saxon strypan, to spoil, to rob.
STRIPT, pp. The older contracted spelling of stripped, retained in the Authorized Version.
To strip a man of office or honour, as well as of garments.
scriptures: Gen 37:3
Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours.
And it came to pass, when Joseph was come unto his brethren, that they stript Joseph out of his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him;
And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead .
And Pharaoh took off his ring from his hand, and put it upon Joseph's hand, and arrayed him in vestures of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck;
corruption_summary: Envy is the least confessed of sins because it disguises itself as a grievance about fairness — which is precisely how Joseph’s brothers justified tearing off his coat.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is envy dressed as justice. No one confesses envy; the emotion always presents itself as a complaint about unfairness, and Joseph’s brothers had a case that would sound reasonable in any age. The father did love him more, the coat was a real provocation, and the boy’s dreams were told without tact. Grant every particular, and the crime remains a crime. What envy does is take a genuine inequity and use it as a warrant, so that the sin feels like a corrective. Scripture is unsparing here: wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy? Wrath burns out; envy is patient, and it waits for the brother to come across the field.

Recover the plain sense: the coat was the father’s to give. That is the answer to every envious grievance — the Giver has a right to be generous where He pleases, and to resent His generosity to another is to arraign Him, not merely the favoured brother. Notice also what God did with the stripping. The coat came off in Dothan and finer vestures went on in Egypt, and the same brothers bowed before them. He does not always reverse an injustice so visibly, but the pattern is instructive: those whom God permits to be stript, He intends to array. The Samaritan who covers the stripped man on the Jericho road is the plainest picture of it.
roots_summary: Saxon strypan, to despoil — robbery of a covering; the first act against Joseph, reversed by Pharaoh’s linen.
roots_lines: Stript — AV contracted spelling of stripped; Saxon strypan, to plunder.
The root sense is robbery, not merely undressing.
Gen 37:23 lingers on the coat: his coat, his coat of many colours, that was on him.
The garment was the token of the father’s love (Gen 37:3).
Reversed in Gen 41:42, where Pharaoh arrays him in fine linen.
usage: The coat is the quarrel: stripping it is the first act of the crime.
Luk 10:30: the stripped man is covered by a Samaritan, not by a priest.
Those whom God permits to be stript, He intends to array.

etymology: From the Latin subornare — sub, secretly or under, and ornare, to furnish or equip. To suborn is to fit a man out privately for a wicked purpose; in law, to procure false testimony by bribe or persuasion.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, at the martyrdom of Stephen: “Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses, and against God” (Act 6:11). The verb is precise and damning. Stephen’s opponents had disputed with him and “were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake” — so, having lost the argument, they equipped witnesses. They did not merely lie; they recruited, briefed, and furnished liars, and then “set up false witnesses” (Act 6:13) before the council. This is the settled procedure of religious men who have run out of arguments, and Scripture shows it twice at least. Jezebel used it against Naboth: “set two men, sons of Belial, before him, to bear witness against him, saying, Thou didst blaspheme God and the king” (1Ki 21:10) — note that the charge, like Stephen’s, is blasphemy, and that the legal forms were scrupulously observed. A fast was proclaimed, elders sat, two witnesses appeared as the law required, and a man was stoned in perfect procedural order. The ninth commandment stands over all of it: “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16). Suborning is that commandment broken at wholesale — the sin of the man who never testifies falsely himself, but arranges for others to.
webster_summary: Procured or bribed to commit perjury or another crime; secretly furnished and instructed for a wicked purpose.
webster_full: SUBORN, v.t. In law, to procure a person to take such a false oath as constitutes perjury.
To procure privately, or by collusion, the commission of a crime.
From the Latin subornare, from sub, under, and ornare, to furnish, deck, equip.
SUBORNED, pp. Procured by bribery or collusion to give false testimony.
The suborner is guilty though he swears nothing himself (Act 6:11).
scriptures: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
And set two men, sons of Belial, before him, to bear witness against him, saying, Thou didst blaspheme God and the king. And then carry him out, and stone him, that he may die.
Act 6:11
Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses, and against God.
Act 6:13
And set up false witnesses, which said, This man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law:
corruption_summary: The suborner’s trade survives wherever a case is built by procuring testimony rather than weighing evidence — and it is most dangerous when, as with Naboth and Stephen, every legal form is scrupulously kept.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is proceduralism without truth. Both scriptural instances of suborning are notable for their correctness. Naboth was tried before elders and nobles, with a proclaimed fast and the two witnesses the law demanded; Stephen was arraigned before the council with witnesses duly set up. Nothing was irregular except that everything was false. This is the abiding warning: legal form is no protection when the men operating it have decided the verdict first, and a society may keep every rule of evidence while making the outcome a foregone conclusion. The modern equivalents need little describing — the sourced allegation, the briefed accuser, the campaign that produces witnesses in the order a narrative requires.

Recover the plain sense: the ninth commandment forbids not only the lie you tell but the lie you arrange. Suborners in Scripture never take the stand. Jezebel wrote letters and sealed them with Ahab’s seal; Stephen’s opponents recruited men and stayed in the crowd. God assigns them the guilt anyway, and Elijah met Ahab in the vineyard with the words Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? though Ahab had thrown no stone. Note finally what suborning is a confession of. They suborned men because they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake. Perjury is the tribute error pays to a truth it cannot answer.
roots_summary: Latin sub + ornare, to equip secretly — to furnish false witnesses; the ninth commandment broken at wholesale.
roots_lines: Suborned — Latin subornare, to furnish or equip under-hand.
In law, to procure another to commit perjury.
Act 6:11: employed against Stephen after his opponents lost the argument.
1Ki 21:10: Jezebel’s two sons of Belial against Naboth — the same charge, blasphemy.
The suborner breaks Exo 20:16 without ever taking an oath himself.
usage: Both biblical cases keep the legal forms exactly — that is what makes them terrifying.
Act 6:10–11: they suborned because they could not resist his wisdom.
Guilt attaches to the arranger as fully as to the perjurer (1Ki 21:19).

etymology: From the Old French ravine, violent seizure, and that from the Latin rapina, plunder — the root of rapine and rapacious. As a verb, to seize and devour with violence; as a noun, the prey so taken.
biblical_def: Ravin is violent seizure, and Scripture uses it of beasts, of men, and of shepherds who are secretly both. Jacob’s blessing on his youngest son is the first instance: “Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at night he shall divide the spoil” (Gen 49:27) — a prophecy fulfilled in the tribe’s fierce warlike history, and, some have thought, in Benjamin’s most famous son, who in the morning of his life made havock of the church and in the evening divided the spoil among the Gentiles. Nahum uses the noun of Nineveh, the lion’s den “filled with prey, and his dens with ravin” (Nah 2:12) — an empire described as a lair heaped with what it has torn. But the gravest use is our Lord’s: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15). Two things are asserted at once — the outward appearance is genuinely sheeplike, and the inward nature is genuinely predatory. The warning would be pointless if the disguise were poor. Ezekiel says the same of Israel’s own rulers: “Her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain” (Eze 22:27). The wolf inside the fold is not a stranger who broke in; he is in the midst thereof.
webster_summary: To seize and devour with violence; also, the prey so seized. Used of beasts of prey and, in our Lord’s warning, of false teachers within the fold.
webster_full: RAVIN, v.i. To prey with rapacity; to seize and devour violently.
RAVIN, n. Prey; plunder; food obtained by violence.
From the Old French ravine; Latin rapina, plunder, from rapere, to seize.
Of the same family as rapine, rapacious, and ravenous.
Ravening, ppr. Preying with rapacity, as a wolf (Mat 7:15).
scriptures: Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at night he shall divide the spoil.
Nah 2:12
The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
Her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain.
corruption_summary: Mat 7:15 is commonly applied only to obvious heretics outside the church, when our Lord’s point is that the wolf is convincingly dressed as a sheep and is standing inside the fold.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is misdirected vigilance. Congregations are taught to watch for false teaching at a distance — the cult on the doorstep, the heresy in another denomination — and are given almost no help identifying a ravening wolf who is orthodox in statement, warm in manner, and already trusted. But our Lord’s warning presumes exactly that. Sheep’s clothing means the disguise works; and Ezekiel puts the wolves in the midst of the city, among her own princes. Paul told the Ephesian elders the same thing with tears: grievous wolves would enter in, not sparing the flock, and also of your own selves shall men arise. The danger is domestic.

Recover the plain sense: our Lord gives the test in the next breath — ye shall know them by their fruits. Not by their eloquence, their following, their results, or their doctrinal statement, but by their fruit, and Ezekiel names the fruit that betrays a wolf: shedding blood, destroying souls, and getting dishonest gain. Where a ministry consistently produces damaged people and enriched leaders, the sheep’s clothing is irrelevant. And note the mercy in the warning: the Shepherd tells the sheep about the wolves. He does not leave His flock to discover them by being eaten.
roots_summary: Latin rapina, plunder — violent seizure; the nature of the wolf beneath the sheep’s clothing.
roots_lines: Ravin — Old French ravine, Latin rapina, plunder, from rapere, to seize.
Kin to rapine, rapacious, and ravenous.
As a noun, the prey itself: his dens with ravin (Nah 2:12).
Gen 49:27: Benjamin ravening as a wolf, morning prey and evening spoil.
Mat 7:15: the clothing is convincing; the nature is predatory.
usage: Mat 7:15 assumes the disguise works — that is why a test is needed.
Eze 22:27 places the ravening wolves among Israel’s own princes.
The test is fruit, and dishonest gain is the fruit that betrays a wolf.

etymology: The older English form of braided, from the Saxon bregdan, to weave or plait. Not to be confused with embroidered, which is needlework upon cloth; broided hair is hair plaited and interwoven, in the ancient fashion, commonly with gold thread and pearls worked into the braid.
biblical_def: The word stands in Paul’s instruction on the adorning of women: “that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array” (1Ti 2:9). The context governs the meaning. In the Ephesus of that day the elaborately plaited coiffure, worked through with gold wire and pearls, was the recognised display of a wealthy woman — expensive, time-consuming, and unmistakably a statement of rank. Paul is not forbidding a plait as such, any more than Peter forbids the wearing of apparel when he writes against “plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel” (1Pe 3:3), for a woman who obeyed that literally would go out unclothed. Both apostles are naming the ostentatious style of their own day in order to strike at the heart behind it. And both immediately supply the substitute, which is the point. Paul says the adorning that becomes women professing godliness is “good works” (1Ti 2:10); Peter says it is the hidden man of the heart, the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. The command is not wear less but adorn yourself with something better, and the standard of value named is God’s own estimate.
webster_summary: Plaited or braided, as hair interwoven in strands; in the apostolic warning, the elaborate and costly coiffure worked with gold and pearls.
webster_full: BROID, v.t. The older form of braid: to weave or plait together, as strands of hair.
From the Saxon bregdan, to weave, to plait, to draw together.
Distinguished from embroider, which is ornamental needlework upon a fabric.
BROIDED, pp. Plaited; interwoven; as, broided hair (1Ti 2:9).
In antiquity, such plaiting was frequently interwoven with gold thread and pearls.
scriptures: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works.
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: The text is pulled in two wrong directions at once — made into a rulebook against braids and jewellery by the strict, and dismissed as cultural residue by the progressive — while the apostolic argument, that adorning is real and must be relocated, is lost by both.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption runs two ways, and the dictionary rejects both. On one side, the legalist reads 1Ti 2:9 as a dress code and produces rules about braids, jewellery, and hemlines that Scripture never gave, making a woman’s godliness measurable by what she has removed. Peter’s parallel exposes the method at once: the same grammar that forbids plaited hair forbids putting on of apparel, and no one supposes the Apostle commanded nakedness. On the other side, progressive readers file the passage under first-century custom and let it say nothing at all — a method which, applied consistently, empties every apostolic instruction on the ground that it was written to somebody in particular. Both evade the same sentence, because both find it easier to argue about hair than about the heart it advertises.

Recover the plain sense: the apostles do not abolish adorning, they relocate it. Every woman will be adorned by something; the question is what she is trusting to make her admired, and at whose expense. Paul answers good works, Peter answers the meek and quiet spirit which is in the sight of God of great price. Note that both give a market valuation. Costly array is costly by the world’s reckoning; the hidden man of the heart is costly by God’s, and He is the buyer whose price stands. That principle judges the wealthy woman’s pearls and the austere woman’s conspicuous plainness with equal force, since a severity displayed for admiration is only broided hair by another name.
roots_summary: Saxon bregdan, to plait — interwoven hair; the apostolic call to relocate adorning from the head to the heart.
roots_lines: Broided — older form of braided; Saxon bregdan, to weave or plait.
Distinct from embroidered, which is needlework upon cloth.
Anciently plaited with gold thread and pearls as a display of rank.
1Ti 2:10 supplies the substitute: good works.
1Pe 3:4 names the price: a meek and quiet spirit, of great price with God.
usage: Peter’s parallel forbids putting on of apparel in the same breath — the sense is comparative, not absolute.
Both apostles name a replacement adorning; neither leaves the woman unadorned.
Conspicuous plainness adopted for admiration is broided hair under another name.

etymology: From tabor, a small hand-drum, through the Old French tabour — ultimately of Persian origin. To taber is to beat as upon a tabor; the word survives in English chiefly in tambourine. In Nah 2:7 it describes women beating upon their own breasts as one beats a drum.
biblical_def: One of the most arresting images in the prophets: “Huzzab shall be led away captive, she shall be brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts” (Nah 2:7). Nineveh has fallen, and her women are led out in a column, moaning like doves and beating their breasts with a rhythmic, drumming grief. The verb is precisely chosen: not merely striking the breast, but tabering — the steady beat of a hand-drum, a funeral cadence keeping time with the march of the captives. The city that had filled her dens with ravin (Nah 2:12), whose merchants were multiplied above the stars of heaven, goes out to the sound of women drumming on their own bodies. Nahum is unsparing because Nineveh had been spared once already; Jonah had preached and the city had repented, and a century later it had returned to blood and cruelty. The next verse presses the desolation further — “Stand, stand, shall they cry; but none shall look back” (Nah 2:8). The beating breast is a universal sign of grief and guilt in Scripture, and it appears again in a very different key when the publican, standing afar off, would not lift so much as his eyes to heaven but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.
webster_summary: Beating as upon a tabor or small drum; used in Scripture of captive women drumming upon their breasts in a cadenced lament.
webster_full: TABOR, n. A small drum, beaten with one stick, used to accompany the pipe.
TABER, v.i. To strike lightly and frequently, as upon a tabor.
From the Old French tabour, a drum; of Eastern origin.
The same root yields tambourine and the surname Taberer, a drummer.
Nah 2:7: tabering upon their breasts, beating them in a rhythmic lament.
scriptures: Nah 2:7
And Huzzab shall be led away captive, she shall be brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts.
Nah 2:8
But Nineveh is of old like a pool of water: yet they shall flee away. Stand, stand, shall they cry; but none shall look back.
Nah 2:12
The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin.
They shall lament for the teats, for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine.
corruption_summary: Nahum is widely avoided as an embarrassment — a prophecy of a city’s destruction with no softening — which quietly denies that God’s judgment on cruelty is itself good news to the cruelly treated.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the editing of God’s severity. Nahum is little preached, and when it is, it is commonly hurried past toward a gentler text, on the assumption that a book celebrating the fall of a city cannot be edifying. But observe who Nineveh was. Nahum calls her the bloody city, full of lies and robbery, whose cruelty had made widows of half the ancient world; the Assyrian records themselves boast of flayings and towers of skulls. The book opens by declaring that the LORD is slow to anger, and great in power — both clauses together — and adds that He is a stronghold in the day of trouble, and He knoweth them that trust in him. Nahum is not a book about God losing His temper. It is a book about God keeping His word to the oppressed.

Recover the plain sense: the tabering women are a real grief and Scripture does not gloat over them; Nahum records the sound rather than mocking it. But a God who never brought Nineveh down would be a God indifferent to everything Nineveh did, and that is not mercy but negligence. The century between Jonah and Nahum is the pointed detail — the city had been spared once on repentance, which proves the judgment was neither hasty nor inevitable. Hold the two books together and you have the whole doctrine: mercy genuinely offered and genuinely refused, and a longsuffering that has an end. The publican’s smitten breast shows the other road; the same gesture, made in time, before the column forms.
roots_summary: From tabor, a hand-drum — to beat rhythmically; in Nahum, captive women drumming upon their breasts as Nineveh falls.
roots_lines: Tabering — from tabor, a small drum; Old French tabour.
Surviving in modern English chiefly as tambourine.
The verb implies a steady, cadenced beat, not a single blow.
Nah 2:7: the maids moan as doves and taber upon their breasts.
Beating the breast is the settled biblical sign of grief and of guilt.
usage: The word supplies a rhythm: a funeral cadence keeping time with the captives’ march.
Nineveh had repented under Jonah a century before — the judgment was neither hasty nor inevitable.
The same gesture, made in time, is the publican’s in Luk 18:13.
